nationality_or_literary_tradition: African American; poet and historian writing in English
literary_identity: African American poet, US Poet Laureate 2012-14, whose first book made the history of her Black and white Mississippi family the subject of a formal and documentary poetry
biography: Natasha Trethewey was born on 26 April 1966 in Gulfport, Mississippi, the daughter of a white professor of English, Eric Trethewey, and a Black social worker, Gwendolyn Ann Turnbough, whose marriage was illegal in Mississippi at the time of her birth. Her mother was murdered by her second husband when Trethewey was nineteen, an event that has been at the centre of much of her work. She took a BA from the University of Georgia, an MA in English and creative writing from Hollins University and an MFA from the University of Massachusetts Amherst, and worked as a professor of history at Emory University before moving to Northwestern. Domestic Work (Graywolf Press, 2000) won the Cave Canem Poetry Prize and was followed by Bellocq's Ophelia (2002), Native Guard (2006), which won the Pulitzer Prize in 2007, Thrall (2012) and Monument (2018). Her memoir Memorial Drive (2020) recounts her mother's murder. She was Poet Laureate of Mississippi from 2012 and US Poet Laureate from 2012 to 2014, and she has edited anthologies of Southern and Civil War poetry.
literary_profile: Domestic Work (2000); Bellocq's Ophelia (2002); Native Guard (2006, Pulitzer 2007); Thrall (2012); Monument: Poems New and Selected (2018); and the memoir Memorial Drive (2020).
stylistic_characteristics: Formal control - the sonnet, the sequence, the persona - used for documentary material; a documentary poetics built from archives, photographs and records; a plain first person that does not raise its voice; and a line that is measured rather than free.
intellectual_concerns: Racial history in Mississippi and Louisiana, including the segregated South and the Civil War; her mother's murder and the failure of the law to protect her; the photographic archive and what it records and omits; and the making of a biracial identity in a state that criminalised it.
historical_significance: Trethewey is the first African American Poet Laureate of Mississippi and the nineteenth US Poet Laureate, and Native Guard is one of the most honoured American poetry books of the 2000s; Domestic Work, her first book, is a landmark of the documentary turn in American poetry at the end of the period, and the Norton's two selections from it introduce that turn through its founding volume.

birthplace: London, United Kingdom; raised in Rhode Island, United States
nationality_or_literary_tradition: Indian American (born in London to Bengali parents); short-story writer and novelist writing in English
literary_identity: Indian American writer whose Interpreter of Maladies won the Pulitzer Prize in 2000 and established the short-story cycle of the South Asian diaspora
biography: Jhumpa Lahiri was born on 11 July 1967 in London to Bengali parents from Calcutta, and the family moved to Kingston, Rhode Island, when she was two. She took a BA from Barnard College, then three master's degrees and a doctorate in Renaissance studies from Boston University. Her first stories appeared in The New Yorker from 1998, and Interpreter of Maladies (Houghton Mifflin, 1999) won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction in 2000 and the PEN/Hemingway Award, making her the first South Asian American writer to win the Pulitzer. The Namesake (2003) was filmed by Mira Nair in 2006, and Unaccustomed Earth (2008) reached the top of the New York Times bestseller list. In 2012 she published In Other Words, a memoir written in Italian, and she has since written and translated in Italian; The Lowland (2013) was shortlisted for the Man Booker Prize, and Whereabouts (2021) was written in Italian and translated by its author. She has taught at Princeton and Barnard.
literary_profile: Interpreter of Maladies (1999); The Namesake (2003); Unaccustomed Earth (2008); The Lowland (2013); In Other Words (2012, in Italian and English); Whereabouts (2021, in Italian); and translations from Italian, including Domenico Starnone's Ties (2016).
stylistic_characteristics: A plain, patient sentence with a long view of its characters; structures of return and recurrence across a collection; Bengali and English in the same household; and an interest in the ordinary accommodations of marriage and migration rather than in crisis.
intellectual_concerns: The South Asian diaspora in America and the second generation's relation to a parents' homeland; marriage, loneliness and the small failures of intimacy; the 1947 partition and its aftermath, in The Lowland; and language and translation, which became the explicit subject of her later work.
historical_significance: Interpreter of Maladies won the Pulitzer Prize in 2000 and made the South Asian American short-story cycle a central form of the period; 'Sexy' - the story the Norton prints - is one of its most anthologised pieces and the story through which the anthology represents the 1990s diaspora writing that reshaped the American short story.

birthplace: Monte Cristi, Dominican Republic; raised in New Jersey, United States
nationality_or_literary_tradition: Dominican American; short-story writer and novelist writing in English
literary_identity: Dominican American writer whose Drown and The Brief Wondrous Life of Oscar Wao brought the immigrant New Jersey of the Dominican diaspora into American fiction and won the Pulitzer Prize in 2008
biography: Junot Díaz was born on 31 December 1968 in Monte Cristi in the Dominican Republic and emigrated at six to Parlin, New Jersey, joining a father he barely knew; he has written about the separation and the poverty of those years. He took a BA from Rutgers University and an MFA from Cornell University, and Drown (Riverhead Books, 1996) collected the stories that made his name, most of them narrated by Yunior, a Dominican American boy in New Jersey. The Brief Wondrous Life of Oscar Wao (Riverhead, 2007) won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction in 2008 and the National Book Critics Circle Award, and This Is How You Lose Her (2012) returned to Yunior. He won a MacArthur Fellowship in 2012, was named chair of the Pulitzer board in 2018, and taught at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. In 2018 he was accused of sexual misconduct by several women, which he acknowledged and apologized for; the allegations have affected his public standing but Drown and Oscar Wao remain standard texts of the Latino and immigrant canon.
literary_profile: Drown (1996); The Brief Wondrous Life of Oscar Wao (2007); This Is How You Lose Her (2012); and the children's book Islandborn (2018).
stylistic_characteristics: A demotic, code-switching narration that moves between Spanish and English without translation; an oral storyteller's digressions, set in footnotes in the novel; a comic voice that keeps the immigrant family's violence in view; and short, blunt sentences in the stories.
intellectual_concerns: The Dominican diaspora in New Jersey and the memory of Trujillo's dictatorship; immigration, absent fathers and serial romance; the racial and class hierarchy inside Latino communities; and the inheritance of history as a curse or a fukú, in the novel's word.
historical_significance: Drown is one of the defining collections of 1990s American fiction and the book through which the Dominican American experience entered the canon; Oscar Wao's Pulitzer in 2008 is usually taken as the arrival of a second generation of Latino writers onto the national stage. The Norton prints the title story of Drown.
